clinicalPearls: A common inherited thrombophilia, second in frequency to factor V Leiden among people of European ancestry, and rare in African and Asian populations
Heterozygotes carry a modestly increased risk of venous thromboembolism, while homozygotes and those who also carry factor V Leiden have a higher risk
The variant tends to present as first venous thrombosis in a young adult, often provoked by an added risk such as combined oral contraception, pregnancy, surgery, or immobility
Plasma prothrombin activity is typically raised, but the diagnosis rests on targeted DNA analysis of the F2 gene rather than a functional assay
Arterial disease association is weak and inconsistent; the variant is chiefly a venous thrombosis risk factor
Detection influences counselling on hormonal contraception, pregnancy, and perioperative thromboprophylaxis more than it dictates the intensity of acute treatment
Family screening is offered selectively, since a positive result in an asymptomatic relative rarely changes management on its own
reference.pathophysiology: The G20210A change lies in the 3' untranslated region of the prothrombin (factor II) gene and acts as a gain-of-function variant that enhances messenger RNA processing and stability. This raises circulating prothrombin concentration, and the excess substrate shifts the coagulation balance towards greater thrombin generation. The resulting mild hypercoagulable state predisposes to venous thromboembolism, with risk amplified when the variant coincides with other inherited or acquired prothrombotic factors.
additionalDifferentials: Factor V Leiden and activated protein C resistance
Acquired provoking states such as malignancy, pregnancy, or oestrogen therapy
additionalInvestigations: Targeted F2 gene analysis to confirm the G20210A variant and distinguish heterozygous from homozygous status
Plasma prothrombin activity, which may be elevated but is not diagnostic
Concurrent factor V Leiden testing to detect combined thrombophilia
Functional assays for antithrombin, protein C and protein S to exclude coexisting deficiencies
Antiphospholipid antibody screen when an acquired thrombophilia is suspected
Objective imaging to confirm and characterise a suspected venous thromboembolic event
redFlags: Extensive or life-threatening venous thromboembolism such as massive pulmonary embolism
Thrombosis at an unusual site such as cerebral, splanchnic, or hepatic veins
Recurrent venous thrombosis despite adequate anticoagulation
Thrombosis in pregnancy or the puerperium suggesting compounded risk
reference.prognosis: Most heterozygous carriers remain asymptomatic throughout life, and thrombotic risk is meaningfully increased only in the presence of additional triggers or coexisting thrombophilia. Long-term outlook depends on the burden of provoking factors and the completeness of anticoagulation after any event.
pitfalls: Interpreting a raised prothrombin level as diagnostic without confirmatory genetic testing
Over-testing asymptomatic relatives when the result will not alter management
Assuming a strong arterial thrombosis link, which the evidence does not support
Neglecting compounded risk when the variant coexists with factor V Leiden or oestrogen exposure
references: Hoffman: Hematology - Basic Principles and Practice
